title: Example pack
description: A small pack that shows the format: one quiz with every question type, one practice exam and one script with two steps.

items.title: Shell basics (example)
items.about: A tiny quiz with one question of every format, to try the importer.

questions.title: Listing files
questions.text: Which command lists the files of the current directory?

options.why: `ls` lists the entries of a directory (the current one by default).
`cd` changes the working directory; it prints nothing.
`pwd` prints the path of the working directory, not its contents.
`cat` prints the contents of files, it does not list a directory.

questions.title: Redirection operators
questions.text: Select every operator that redirects standard output.

options.why: Sends standard output to a file, replacing it.
Sends standard output to a file, appending.
Reads standard input from a file; it does not redirect output.
Connects the output of one command to the input of another; no file is involved.

questions.title: Exit status
questions.text: After a successful command, `$?` is `{{0}}`; after a failed one it is a number other than `{{0}}`... and `$#` is the number of {{1}}.
questions.note: `$?` holds the exit status of the last command.

wrong.why: 1 is a common failure code, not the success code.

items.why: There is nothing to run before it exists.
Without the execute bit it cannot be started directly.
Only an executable script can be started this way.

questions.title: Standard streams
questions.text: Match each stream with its number.

items.why: It must change the shell's own directory.

items.title: Basics exam (example)
items.about: Ten single-choice questions to try the importer.

questions.title: Print the working directory
questions.text: Which command prints the path of the current directory?

options.why: It prints the absolute path of the working directory.
It lists entries, not the path.
It changes directory and prints nothing.
Not the standard way to print the path.

questions.title: Append to a file
questions.text: Which operator appends standard output to a file?

options.why: It opens the file for appending.
It truncates the file first.
It reads input from a file.
It feeds another command, not a file.

questions.title: Exit status of success
questions.text: What is the exit status of a command that succeeded?

options.why: By convention 0 means success.
Usually a generic failure.
Exit statuses are 0-255; -1 is not used.
That is a failure code.

questions.title: Number of arguments
questions.text: Which variable holds the number of arguments of a script?

options.why: It expands to the count of positional parameters.
The exit status of the last command.
The process id of the shell.
The name of the script.

questions.title: Make a script executable
questions.text: Which command makes `run.sh` executable for its owner?

options.why: It adds the execute bit for the user.
It removes every permission.
`chown` changes the owner, not the mode.
It would try to run it, replacing the shell.

questions.title: Count lines
questions.text: Which command counts the lines of `data.txt`?

options.why: `-l` counts lines.
`-w` counts words.
`-c` counts bytes.
It numbers lines but also prints the whole file.

questions.title: Search a pattern
questions.text: Which command prints the lines of `log` containing `error`?

options.why: `grep` prints the matching lines.
`find` searches for files, not text.
`cut` selects fields of lines.
It just prints the words.

options.t: Sends the output of `a` to the input of `b`
options.why: The pipe connects the two commands.
They run together, connected.

options.t: Saves the output of `a` in a file called `b`
options.why: That is `a > b`.
That is `a || b`.

questions.title: Variable use
questions.text: How do you print the value of the variable `name`?

options.why: The `$` expands the variable.
It prints the word name.
Braces without `$` are literal.
`print` is not a shell command here.

questions.title: Test a file
questions.text: Which test is true when `f` is a regular file?

options.why: `-f` tests for a regular file.
`-d` tests for a directory.
`-z` tests for an empty string.
`-n` tests for a non-empty string; it says nothing about files.

items.title: Counting files
items.cmds: find -maxdepth 1 -type f, wc -l, test -d, exit codes

steps.title: Count the files
steps.readme:
Write `count.sh DIR`. It prints how many **regular files** are directly inside `DIR` (hidden files count, files in subdirectories and directories do not). Print only the number.

Example: for a directory with `a.txt`, `.hidden` and a subdirectory `sub`, it prints `2`.

steps.title: The usual checks
steps.readme: Checks: not exactly one argument → an error message **and the correct usage** (e.g. `Usage: count.sh dir`) on standard error, exit **1**; the path does not exist → an error naming it, exit **2**; it exists but is not a directory → an error naming it, exit **3**. Otherwise as before.
